::: {.callout-important title="Status of this document"}
This methods document describes the direct peak models as they are implemented in `idmodels` (module `idmodels.peak`: `series.py`, `revision.py`, `base.py`, `baseline.py`, `gbqr.py`, `kcde.py`; configuration classes `PeakModelConfig`, `PeakBaselineModelConfig`, `PeakGBQRModelConfig` and `PeakKCDEModelConfig` in `idmodels/config.py`) and in the sandbox scripts `src/peak_*` and `analysis/peak-models/*.py`. Every specific setting is stated in a callout titled *Implementation*, with the name of the configuration field that controls it where one exists. Three models are implemented: the conditional-climatology baseline (`peak_baseline`), gradient-boosted direct models (`peak_gbqr`), and kernel conditional density estimation (`peak_kcde`). The hierarchical Bayesian model and the ensembles are **planned but not yet implemented**; their sections are labelled as such. Design choices that were considered but not implemented appear in remarks titled *Alternatives considered*. The document contains **no results**.
:::

# The problem in plain terms {#sec-problem}

## Influenza seasons

Influenza ("flu") circulates in the United States every year, but in the temperate Northern Hemisphere most transmission happens in a few months between roughly October and May. A typical year has one dominant wave of infections that rises over several weeks, reaches a maximum, and then declines. The timing and the height of that maximum vary a lot from year to year (depending on which virus strains circulate, prior immunity, vaccination, and behavior) and from place to place within a year. Some years have two waves, for example when two different influenza types dominate at different times.

Because this annual cycle straddles the calendar new year, surveillance data are organized into **seasons** that run from late summer of one year to late summer of the next (defined precisely in @sec-time).

## Hospital admissions reported to NHSN

The quantity we forecast comes from the **National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN)**, a CDC system to which US hospitals report data. Each week, hospitals report the number of newly admitted patients who have a laboratory-confirmed influenza infection. These counts are added up by **jurisdiction** (each of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico) and nationally. We call the jurisdiction-level weekly total the **weekly incident influenza hospital admissions**, or just **incidence**.

Two features of these data matter throughout this document:

1. **They are revised.** The number first published for a given week is often incomplete, because some hospitals report late or correct earlier reports. The published value for that week changes in later releases. This is called **backfill**, and it is the subject of @sec-backfill.
2. **The usable history is short.** Consistent jurisdiction-level NHSN influenza admissions data are available for only about four complete seasons (2022/23 through 2025/26). That is too few seasons to learn much about the timing and size of season peaks from NHSN alone. We therefore borrow historical information from two older surveillance systems (@sec-data).

## FluSight and the forecasting calendar

**FluSight** is CDC's collaborative influenza forecasting challenge. Each week during the season, participating teams submit probabilistic forecasts to a public repository (a "forecast hub") in a standardized file format (the *Hubverse* format). FluSight has run in some form since the 2013/14 season. Its earlier rounds forecast ILINet data (described in @sec-data) and included seasonal peak targets (McGowan et al. 2019; Reich et al. 2019); since 2021/22 its main target has been laboratory-confirmed influenza hospital admissions (Mathis et al. 2024). The weekly schedule is as follows.

- Forecasts are due on a **Wednesday**.
- The **reference date** $r$ is the Saturday following that Wednesday. It labels the submission round.
- At submission time, the most recently published NHSN data usually cover weeks up to and including the week that ended on the Saturday $r - 7$ days. We call that latest reported week $t$. Its value is itself provisional and will usually be revised upward.

The main FluSight target asks for forecasts of weekly incidence at **horizons** $h \in \{-1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$, meaning the week that ends on the Saturday $r + 7h$ days. Horizon $-1$ is the latest reported week $t$ (its value is known, but only provisionally). Horizon $0$ is the week that ends on the reference date, which is under way when the forecast is made but not yet reported. An estimate of a quantity that refers to the present or recent past but has not yet been observed (or not finally observed) is called a **nowcast**. Horizons $1$ to $3$ are true forecasts of the future.

## The two seasonal targets and why they matter

In addition to the weekly target, FluSight 2026/27 asks for two optional **seasonal targets** for each of 53 locations (the US, the 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico).

- **Peak week** (`peak week inc flu hosp`): which week of the season will have the highest weekly count of influenza hospital admissions? The forecast is a **probability mass function (pmf)**: a probability for each of the 34 Saturdays from 2026-10-10 to 2027-05-29, which must sum to 1.
- **Peak size** (`peak inc flu hosp`): how large will that highest weekly count be? The forecast consists of 23 **quantiles** of the predictive distribution of this count, at levels $0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, \dots, 0.90, 0.95, 0.975, 0.99$.

For both targets, the `horizon` and `target_end_date` columns of the submission are left missing (`NA`), since the targets refer to the season as a whole rather than to a single week. Teams are asked to keep submitting after the peak appears to have passed; at that point a good forecast puts almost all of its probability on the week that has been observed to be the maximum, and puts the peak-size quantiles close to the observed maximum.

These targets matter to public health because the peak is when hospitals are most strained. Knowing roughly *when* the peak will come helps with staffing, bed planning, and the timing of communications; knowing *how large* it will be helps judge whether capacity will be sufficient.

## Why "direct" models

There are two broad ways to produce these forecasts.

1. **Trajectory-based.** Build a model that simulates the whole remaining season week by week, draw many simulated seasons, and compute the peak week and peak size of each draw. This is conceptually clean, but it requires a model whose joint distribution over many weeks ahead (sometimes 30 or more) is well calibrated. Weekly forecasting models are usually built and checked only for a few weeks ahead, and their long-range joint behavior is rarely trustworthy.
2. **Direct.** Treat the peak week and peak size themselves as the response variables, and learn their conditional distribution given a summary of the season observed so far. This targets exactly the quantities that are scored, and it can use long historical records in which the outcome of each season is known.

This document describes direct models. Their main cost is that timing and size are modeled as two separate marginal distributions, so the two forecasts need not come from one joint distribution. FluSight scores the two targets separately, so this is acceptable. (In the KCDE model of @sec-kcde both marginals come from the same set of weighted analogs, so a joint distribution is available in principle, but the implementation uses only the two marginals. The planned hierarchical model of @sec-hier would be fully joint.)

# Notation and target definitions {#sec-notation}

## Time: epidemiological weeks, seasons, and the window {#sec-time}

**Epidemiological weeks.** CDC counts time in **MMWR weeks** (also called epidemiological weeks, or epiweeks). Each MMWR week runs from Sunday to Saturday. Week 1 of a year is the first Sunday-to-Saturday week that has at least four days in that calendar year, so a year has either 52 or 53 MMWR weeks. We label every week by the date of its final Saturday, its **week-ending date**.

**Seasons.** Following the `iddata` package, the season labeled $s = $ "YYYY/YY" (for example "2026/27") starts with MMWR week 31 of year YYYY (late July or early August) and ends with MMWR week 30 of the following year.

**Season week.** The **season week** $\omega(w) \in \{1, \dots, 53\}$ of a week $w$ counts weeks from the start of its season: MMWR week 31 is season week 1. Concretely, if $w$ is MMWR week $\mathrm{ew}$ of calendar year $\mathrm{yr}$, then $\omega(w) = \mathrm{ew} - 30$ when $\mathrm{ew} > 30$, and $\omega(w) = \mathrm{ew} - 30 + E(\mathrm{yr}-1)$ when $\mathrm{ew} \le 30$, where $E(\mathrm{yr}-1) \in \{52, 53\}$ is the number of MMWR weeks in year $\mathrm{yr} - 1$. Season week places different seasons on a common axis.

**Convention: weeks are season weeks.** Within a season, the map $w \mapsto \omega(w)$ is one-to-one, so from here on we identify each week with its season week: $t$, $u$ and $w$ denote integers in $\{1, \dots, 53\}$, and $w + m$ is the week $m$ weeks after $w$. The implementation stores every (source, location, season) series as a row of an array with one column per season week, and works entirely in this index.

**The window.** The peak targets are defined only over a fixed set of weeks, the **window**
$$
\mathcal{W} = \{\underline\omega, \underline\omega + 1, \dots, \overline\omega\}, \qquad \underline\omega = 10, \quad \overline\omega = 43.
$$
For 2026/27 these are the Saturdays 2026-10-10 (MMWR week 40 of 2026) through 2027-05-29 (MMWR week 21 of 2027). We write $n_{\mathcal{W}} = \overline\omega - \underline\omega + 1 = 34$ for the number of window weeks.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Window.** `PeakModelConfig.window_start_week = 10` and `window_end_week = 43`, in season weeks, for every season and every data source. For the four seasons with FluSight peak tasks in `hub-config/tasks.json` (2023/24, 2024/25, 2025/26, 2026/27), the 34 pmf dates are exactly season weeks 10 through 43, including 2025/26, which follows the 53-week MMWR year 2025. Output dates are generated from season weeks by `season_week_to_date`.
:::

**Reference date and latest observed week.** The reference date $r$ is a Saturday. For each location, the implementation takes $t$ to be the latest season week with a reported count in the most recent NHSN vintage released on or before $r$ (vintages are defined below). Usually $t$ is the week one week before $r$. Everything the model knows about the current season ends at $t$, so we index forecasts by $t$. The first 2026/27 reference date is $r = $ 2026-10-10, so the first $t$ is 2026-10-03 (season week 9), which is *before* the window starts.

## Locations, populations, and rates

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the set of 53 forecast locations and let $l \in \mathcal{L}$ index them. Let $N_{l}$ be the population of location $l$ in the season under consideration. Let $c_{l,w}$ be the NHSN count of influenza admissions in location $l$ during week $w$, and define the **rate per 100,000 population**
$$
y_{l,w} = 10^5 \, \frac{c_{l,w}}{N_l}.
$$
Rates make locations of very different sizes comparable (California has about 70 times the population of Wyoming), so all models work with rates and convert back to counts only when writing a submission (@sec-submission). The population is fixed within a season, so a rate series and its count series have the same ordering of weeks and therefore the same peak week.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Populations.** $N_l$ is the US Census estimate for location $l$ and season $s$ from `iddata` (`_load_us_census`, exposed as the ancillary `PopulationData`). The same estimate is used by `iddata` to form historical NHSN rates and by the peak models to form current-season rates and to convert peak-size rates back to counts, so the round trip is exact. For the current season, the population of that season is used if available, and otherwise that of the most recent season with a population estimate. Locations without current-season data or a population are omitted from the submission with a warning.
:::

## Data vintages and backfill

Because NHSN data are revised, "the value for week $w$" is not a single number. We write $c^{(a)}_{l,w}$ and $y^{(a)}_{l,w}$ for the count and rate of week $w$ **as reported in the data release published on date $a$**. The date $a$ is called the **as-of date**, and the data set as published on that date is called a **vintage**. Let $t_l(a)$ be the latest week reported for location $l$ in vintage $a$. The **reporting lag** of week $w$ in vintage $a$ is $j = t_l(a) - w \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ weeks; the newest week in a release has lag $0$.

We write $c^{(\infty)}_{l,w}$ and $y^{(\infty)}_{l,w}$ for the **final** value, meaning the value after revisions have settled. Operationally, "final" always means the value in the latest vintage available at the time in question (@sec-backfill, @sec-eval). The difference between an early-vintage value and the final value is the **backfill** or **revision**.

## The information set and the forecasting problem

At reference date $r$, the forecaster knows the information set $\mathcal{F}_t$, which contains:

- all NHSN vintages with as-of date $a \le r$; in particular the most recent one, with as-of date $a_r$, gives the current season's reported values $\{c^{(a_r)}_{l,w} : l \in \mathcal{L},\, w \le t\}$;
- the other data sources (@sec-data), which are not versioned; and
- the records of all past seasons as available on $r$.

From the forecaster's point of view the targets are **random variables**, because they depend on data that have not yet been observed and on revisions that have not yet been made. A probabilistic forecast is an estimate of the **conditional distribution** of a target given $\mathcal{F}_t$. For a generic real-valued target $T$ we write its conditional distribution function as $F_T(v \mid \mathcal{F}_t) = \Pr(T \le v \mid \mathcal{F}_t)$ and its conditional **quantile function** as
$$
Q_T(\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_t) = \inf\{ v : F_T(v \mid \mathcal{F}_t) \ge \tau \}, \qquad \tau \in (0,1).
$$
For a discrete target such as the peak week, the conditional distribution is described by its pmf.

## The two targets

Fix a location $l$ and season $s$ and suppress them from the notation. The **peak week** is the window week with the largest final count,
$$
W^* = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{w \in \mathcal{W}} \; c^{(\infty)}_{w},
$$ {#eq-peak-week}
and the **peak size** is the corresponding maximum,
$$
C^* = \max_{w \in \mathcal{W}} c^{(\infty)}_w, \qquad Y^* = 10^5 \, C^* / N = \max_{w \in \mathcal{W}} y^{(\infty)}_w .
$$ {#eq-peak-size}
$C^*$ is the peak on the count scale (the submitted scale) and $Y^*$ is the same quantity on the rate scale (the modeling scale).

**Tie rule.** If two or more window weeks share the maximal final count, $W^*$ is not unique. FluSight's rule is that peak-week forecasts for that location are then *not scored*. The peak size $C^*$ is still well defined and is still scored. Ties are judged on integer counts, so they are most plausible in small jurisdictions with low counts. When a single week is needed (in training), the implementation takes the **earliest** week attaining the maximum.

**What is submitted.** For the peak week, the forecast is a pmf $p_t(w) \approx \Pr(W^* = w \mid \mathcal{F}_t)$ for $w \in \mathcal{W}$, with $p_t(w) \ge 0$ and $\sum_{w \in \mathcal{W}} p_t(w) = 1$. For the peak size, the forecast is the set of values $q_t(\tau) \approx Q_{C^*}(\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_t)$ for the 23 levels $\tau \in \mathcal{T} = \{0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, \dots, 0.90, 0.95, 0.975, 0.99\}$.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Peak size is defined over the window.** The FluSight README describes peak incidence as the highest weekly count "during any epidemiological week of the season". Both in training (`series.season_peaks`) and in evaluation (`build_peak_oracle.py`), $C^*$ is the maximum over the same 34 window weeks used for the peak week, and $W^*$ is the earliest week attaining it. The two definitions differ only if a season's maximum falls outside the window, which is rare for influenza. This should be checked against the FluSight evaluation code when it is released.
:::

# Data sources {#sec-data}

## NHSN hospital admissions (the target source)

NHSN counts are what the targets are defined on. Through `iddata`, NHSN data can be loaded **as of** any past date, which returns the vintage published on that date. Vintages before 2024-11-15 come from an archive of an earlier federal (HHS) reporting system, and later vintages come from NHSN itself. Consistent jurisdiction-level history covers the seasons 2022/23 to 2025/26. `iddata` converts counts to rates per 100,000 using census population estimates for the corresponding season.

NHSN is the only one of our sources for which past vintages are available, so it is the only one from which we can learn how revisions behave (@sec-backfill).

## ILINet, scaled by percent positive

**ILINet** is CDC's outpatient surveillance network. Participating clinics report the total number of patient visits each week and the number of those visits for **influenza-like illness (ILI)**, which is defined by symptoms (roughly, fever together with a cough or sore throat) rather than by a laboratory test. The weekly **percent ILI** is the fraction of visits that were for ILI, expressed as a percentage. At the national and regional levels this percentage is weighted by state population ("weighted ILI"); at the state level `iddata` uses the unweighted percentage.

ILI is not specific to influenza, because other respiratory viruses cause the same symptoms. To make the signal more specific, `iddata` multiplies percent ILI by the **percent positive**: the percentage of respiratory specimens tested by clinical laboratories (reported to the WHO and NREVSS laboratory systems) that were positive for influenza in that week. The product (divided by 100) approximates the percentage of outpatient visits that were due to influenza. We refer to this product as **ILINet** from here on.

ILINet data go back to the 1997/98 season for the 10 **HHS regions** (groupings of states used by the US Department of Health and Human Services) and the nation, and to about 2010 for individual states. For the earliest seasons (1997/98 to 2001/02) `iddata` keeps only season weeks 10 to 42. `iddata` does not provide vintages for ILINet, so only final values are available.

## FluSurv-NET

**FluSurv-NET** is a population-based surveillance system for laboratory-confirmed influenza hospitalizations in defined catchment areas (selected counties) in about 14 sites across the country. It reports weekly hospitalization rates per 100,000 catchment residents. `iddata` loads seasons 2010/11 to 2022/23, maps the sites to states (two New York sites are averaged into one New York series) and the "Entire Network" to the US.

Because not all hospitalized flu patients are tested, FluSurv-NET rates undercount true hospitalizations, and the degree of undercounting varies by season. With `burden_adj=True` (the default used here), `iddata` multiplies every weekly rate in season $s$ by a season-specific factor, the ratio of CDC's estimated total national influenza hospitalization burden for season $s$ to the cumulative hospitalizations implied by the network's cumulative rate. This makes the level of different seasons more comparable. Like ILINet, FluSurv-NET is not versioned in `iddata`.

## Why the sources are on different scales, and what is comparable

The three sources measure different things: NHSN measures admissions per 100,000 residents in all reporting hospitals, ILINet measures a percentage of outpatient visits, and FluSurv-NET measures hospitalizations per 100,000 residents of selected counties. Their absolute levels are therefore not directly comparable, and the ratio between them differs by location and season. What they do share is the *shape* of a season: when it starts to rise, when it peaks, and how large the peak is relative to what came before. This is why all our models work with relative quantities (@sec-relative).

| Source | Quantity | Units | Seasons (approx.) | Geography | Vintages |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NHSN | lab-confirmed flu admissions | rate per 100k | 2022/23 to 2025/26 | 53 locations | yes |
| ILINet × percent positive | flu-attributable share of outpatient visits | percent | 1997/98+ (regions, US); about 2010+ (states) | US, HHS regions, states | no |
| FluSurv-NET (burden adjusted) | lab-confirmed flu hospitalizations | rate per 100k (adjusted) | 2010/11 to 2022/23 | about 14 sites mapped to states, plus US | no |

## Scales, offsets, and data preparation {#sec-transforms}

The peak models use each source on its **native scale** (rates per 100,000 for NHSN and FluSurv-NET, percent for ILINet) and take logarithms after adding a small source-specific **offset** $\varepsilon_g > 0$, which keeps logs finite when a value is zero. No other transformation is applied: in particular, none of the fourth-root, source-floor and center-and-scale transformations used by the `idmodels` weekly models. Every feature and target is a log ratio of two values of the same series, or a count of weeks (@sec-relative, @sec-features), so no scale factor is needed. A side benefit is that a known leakage issue of the weekly models does not arise here: `CenterScaleTransform` computes its factors from all available data for a (source, location), including the season being predicted, and for peak targets this would leak information about the peak itself. Because the peak models never use those factors, the issue does not apply.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Offsets and data preparation** (`series.LOG_EPS`, `series.build_season_arrays`, `PeakModelConfig`).

- $\varepsilon_{\text{NHSN}} = 0.01$ per 100,000; $\varepsilon_{\text{FluSurv}} = 0.01$ per 100,000; $\varepsilon_{\text{ILINet}} = 0.001$ (percent). Each is roughly 1/1000 of a typical national peak of that source. These are *not* the source floors of `idmodels/constants.py`.
- Each (source, aggregation level, location, season) series is laid out by season week 1 to 53. Interior missing values are filled by linear interpolation, but only for gaps of at most 2 consecutive missing weeks (`max_gap = 2`); longer gaps, and leading and trailing missing values, stay missing.
- Pandemic seasons (2008/09, 2009/10, 2020/21, 2021/22) have their values set to missing by `iddata` (`DiseaseDataLoader.load(drop_pandemic_seasons=True)`), for every source, so they never enter training.
- A historical series is used only if it has at least `min_window_obs = 25` non-missing window weeks (after interpolation).
- The supplementary sources are `supplementary_sources = [ILINet, FluSurv-NET]`; the target is always NHSN.
:::

# Conditioning on the season so far {#sec-relative}

All models share one idea: instead of predicting $W^*$ and $Y^*$ directly, predict how they relate to what has already been observed.

## Summaries of the observed season

Consider one series (one source, location and season) observed through week $t$, with values $x_1, \dots, x_t$ in the source's units, some possibly missing. For the current NHSN season, $x_u = y^{(a_r)}_u$ is the currently reported rate. Let $\bar x_u$ be the **forward-filled** series: the most recent non-missing value among $x_1, \dots, x_u$ (missing if there is none). Let
$$
\mathcal{O}_t = \{u \in \mathcal{W} : u \le t,\; x_u \text{ not missing}\}
$$
be the window weeks already observed. Define

- the **running maximum** $M_t = \max_{u \in \mathcal{O}_t} x_u$;
- the week at which it occurred, $A_t$, the **earliest** $u \in \mathcal{O}_t$ with $x_u = M_t$; and
- the number of **weeks since the maximum**, $d_t = t - A_t \ge 0$.

When we condition on $\mathcal{F}_t$, all three are known constants, not random variables. We also write $\ell^M_t = \log(M_t + \varepsilon)$ for the log running maximum.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Convention when $\mathcal{O}_t$ is empty** (`series.running_max`). At the first reference dates of a season $\mathcal{O}_t$ is empty, because $t < \underline\omega$ (for 2026/27 this is the case at $r = $ 2026-10-10). Then $M_t = \bar x_t$, the latest available value, and $A_t = t$, so $d_t = 0$. In this case $z$ (below) can be negative, and the models allow that; the "already peaked" class is excluded (@sec-classes-to-pmf).
:::

## The relative size target $z$

**The question the models answer.** A public health planner who looks at the admissions curve partway through a season asks: *how much higher will this get?* The biggest week so far, $M_t$, is known. What is uncertain is the growth still to come. The models are built around exactly that quantity, the remaining growth of the running maximum on the log scale:
$$
z = \log \frac{Y^* + \varepsilon}{M_t + \varepsilon},
$$ {#eq-z}
where $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_g$ is a small offset for the series' source (@sec-transforms). For example, $z = \log 2 \approx 0.69$ means "the season's peak will be twice the largest week seen so far", and $z = 0$ means "the largest week so far is the peak".

**Why not predict the peak $Y^*$ directly?** There are three reasons, each specific to this problem.

1. *The training data come from sources that are not on a common scale.* NHSN, the target source, covers only three or four usable seasons, so the models also learn from about 25 seasons of ILINet and 11 of FluSurv-NET (@sec-data). These measure different things in different units: a weighted percentage of outpatient visits scaled by laboratory positivity, and hospitalization rates in selected counties. A peak of "12" means nothing across them. A peak "twice the current maximum" means roughly the same thing in every source, because $z$ does not change when a series and its offset are multiplied by a constant. Predicting $z$ lets the long histories be pooled without first mapping every source onto the NHSN scale, which is difficult and would itself add uncertainty.
2. *Remaining growth depends mainly on the stage of the epidemic, which the data reveal; the absolute peak depends mainly on population size and season severity, which they largely do not.* A location whose admissions are still doubling every week, one whose growth is slowing, and one that has been falling for a month call for very different forecasts of $z$, whatever their size. The features of @sec-features describe that stage (weeks since the maximum, recent growth, level relative to the maximum). The conditional distribution of $z$ given those features is therefore much more similar across locations, seasons and sources than the distribution of $Y^*$, so one model can be shared by all of them.
3. *The scale builds in what we know for certain.* Once the data are final the season's peak can never be lower than the largest week already seen, so $z \ge 0$, and $z = 0$ exactly when the peak has already passed (@sec-relative, "What these targets look like when the data are final"). Forecasts made on this scale cannot fall below the observed maximum. They also shrink onto the observed maximum after the peak, as FluSight requires, because the training data contain many post-peak rows with $z = 0$. No hand-written rule is needed for either behavior.

**Converting back to the peak.** FluSight asks for quantiles of the peak itself, in admissions, so every $z$ forecast has to be converted back. Given $\mathcal{F}_t$, the map
$$
\psi_t(z) = (M_t + \varepsilon)e^{z} - \varepsilon
$$
recovers $Y^* = \psi_t(z)$. It has known coefficients and is continuous and strictly increasing. Quantiles are **equivariant** under such maps: for any random variable $Z$ and any continuous, strictly increasing function $\psi$, the $\tau$-quantile of $\psi(Z)$ is $\psi$ applied to the $\tau$-quantile of $Z$. Therefore
$$
Q_{Y^*}(\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_t) = (M_t + \varepsilon)\exp\{Q_z(\tau \mid \mathcal{F}_t)\} - \varepsilon,
$$ {#eq-z-invert}
and modeling the quantiles of $z$ is exactly equivalent to modeling the quantiles of $Y^*$. The equivalence holds for quantiles but not for means, since $E[e^{Z}] \ne e^{E[Z]}$. This is one reason the whole approach is built on quantiles. The final step multiplies the rate by the location's population divided by $10^5$ to give counts (@sec-submission).

Two details complete the picture. First, the offset $\varepsilon$ exists so that the logarithm is defined when a week has zero admissions. It is set to about one thousandth of a typical national peak in each source's units, which keeps $z$ comparable across sources, and the same value is used in @eq-z and @eq-z-invert. Second, with real NHSN data $M_t$ is not quite known, because recent weeks are revised after they are first reported. In practice @eq-z-invert is therefore applied separately to each simulated final version of the season, each with its own running maximum $\tilde M_t$. The reported quantiles are those of the pooled draws, which is the quantile of a mixture and not an average of quantiles (@sec-mc).

**Where this scale works badly.** Very early in a season $M_t$ is close to zero, so $z$ is large, highly variable and nearly uninformative. Among all training rows the 97.5% quantile of $z$ is about 7.4, a growth factor of roughly 1,600. The forecast then rests mostly on $\varepsilon$ and on level features such as the location's past peaks. This extreme early-season range also affects fitting, as discussed for GBQR in @sec-gbqr.

## The relative timing target $k$ and the timing classes

Define the **timing offset** $k = W^* - t$, in weeks. Then $k \le 0$ means the peak week is one of the already-observed weeks, $k = 1$ means the peak is the week ending on the reference date, and so on. The individual past weeks are not distinguished, so all models work with the **timing class**
$$
k^+ = \max(k, 0) \in \{0, 1, \dots, k_{\max}\}, \qquad k_{\max} = \overline\omega - 1 = 42 .
$$
Class $0$ means "the peak has already happened"; class $j \ge 1$ means "the peak is $j$ weeks after $t$". The upper limit $k_{\max}$ is the largest offset that can occur, since $W^* \le \overline\omega$ and $t \ge 1$. A model's timing output is a vector of class probabilities $(\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots, \pi_{k_{\max}})$. How the class-0 probability is placed on specific past weeks is handled by the shared backfill step of @sec-backfill.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Timing classes** (`PeakModel`, attribute `kmax = window_end_week - 1`). All models return probabilities over the $k_{\max} + 1 = 43$ classes. The baseline and KCDE estimate every class directly. GBQR models only the classes $0, 1, \dots, K$ individually, with $K$ = `PeakGBQRModelConfig.max_k` = 12, plus one tail class "$k > K$", which it spreads over later classes by climatology (@sec-gbqr).
:::

## What these targets look like when the data are final

To see why this parameterization is useful, suppose for a moment that the currently reported values were already final ($x_u = y^{(\infty)}_u$) and $\mathcal{O}_t$ is not empty. Then three facts hold exactly.

1. $z \ge 0$, because the season maximum is at least the maximum so far.
2. $z = 0$ if and only if $k \le 0$: if the peak has already happened, then $Y^* = M_t$; if it has not, then (because $W^*$ is the earliest week attaining the maximum) some future week strictly exceeds $M_t$.
3. $W^* \in \{A_t\} \cup \{u \in \mathcal{W} : u > t\}$: a past week that is not the current (earliest) maximum cannot be the season peak.

So the distribution of $z$ has an **atom** (a point mass) at $0$ whose size equals $\Pr(k \le 0)$, plus a continuous part on $(0, \infty)$. Every model below can represent this.

With real, revisable NHSN data, none of the three facts is exact for the currently reported values. A past week that currently looks smaller than $M_t$ can be revised upward and become the peak, and $M_t$ itself can be revised. These departures are small but, for the log score, important. They are handled in @sec-backfill by applying the models to simulated *final* versions of the current season, to which the three facts do apply.

## Why condition on the season so far

**It makes the sources comparable.** The timing offset $k$ depends only on the *ordering* of the weeks, so it is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of a series, including a change of units. The size ratio $z$ is unchanged if a series and $\varepsilon$ are multiplied by the same constant. So $k$ and $z$ mean roughly the same thing in NHSN, ILINet and FluSurv-NET, and the long histories can be used without first calibrating their absolute levels to NHSN.

**It handles the whole season with no special cases.** Early in the season $\Pr(k \le 0)$ is near zero, and the distributions of $k$ and $z$ are wide. After the peak, the training data contain many rows in which $M_t$ was the eventual peak, and the models learn to put most of the probability on $k \le 0$ and $z = 0$. The forecasts then collapse onto the observed peak, as FluSight asks, without any hand-coded rule.

**It builds in the logical constraints.** Peak-size quantiles computed with @eq-z-invert from nonnegative $z$ quantiles cannot fall below the (simulated final) observed maximum, and past non-maximal weeks receive only the probability justified by revisions.

**A known weakness.** Early in a season the size target $z$ is large and nearly uninformative, because $M_t$ is close to zero. See the end of the discussion of $z$ above, and @sec-gbqr for its consequence for fitting.

# Training by season replay {#sec-replay}

## Constructing the training rows

Direct models need many examples of the form "what the season looked like at week $t$" paired with "what the peak turned out to be". We create them by **replaying** every completed historical season. For each source $g$, location $l$ (including national and, for ILINet, HHS-region series), season $s$, and **forecast origin** $t$, we create one training row $i = (g, l, s, t)$ with

- **features** $\phi_i$, computed only from the series truncated at week $t$ (and from the national series of the same source and season truncated at $t$, and from strictly earlier seasons); and
- **targets** $z_i$, $k_i$ and $k^+_i = \max(k_i, 0)$, computed from the completed season with @eq-peak-week, @eq-peak-size and @eq-z, with the peak taken only over the window.

All historical values, including NHSN's, are the values **as available on the reference date** (for past seasons these are essentially final). Training therefore learns the relationship between the features of a *final* series and its outcome. Real-time data and their revisions enter only for the current season, through the simulation of final values in @sec-backfill.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Season replay** (`series.build_replay_rows`, `PeakModel._fit_if_needed`).

- **Training seasons: forward chaining.** Only seasons strictly before the forecast season are used (`inputs.data["season"] < season`), for every source. There is no leave-one-season-out training.
- **Data vintage.** All training data are loaded with `DiseaseDataLoader().load(..., as_of=r)`; for NHSN this is the single vintage available on $r$, and ILINet and FluSurv-NET are unversioned.
- **Series used.** Only series with at least `min_window_obs = 25` observed window weeks.
- **Origins.** $t = 5, 6, \dots, 43$ (`replay_start_week = 5` through `window_end_week`), keeping a row only if $x_t$ itself is observed (not merely forward-filled).
- **Refitting.** Because training uses only earlier seasons, the fitted model changes only with the season. A model object is fitted once per (season, set of quantile levels) and reused for later reference dates of that season. In the hindcasts (`run_hindcasts.py`) the fit therefore uses the historical data loaded at the first reference date processed in each season.
:::

## Features {#sec-features}

Features describe the series as observed through week $t$ and are scale-free (log ratios and week counts). They use $\bar x$ (forward-filled values) and the log values $\ell_u = \log(\bar x_u + \varepsilon)$, with $\ell^M_t$, $A_t$ and $d_t$ as in @sec-relative. A feature is missing if any value it needs is missing (for example, $\ell_{t-3}$ when fewer than 4 weeks exist).

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Feature list** (`series.state_features`; column names in `code font`).

| Feature | Definition |
|---|---|
| `season_week` | $t$ |
| `rel_max` | $\ell_t - \ell^M_t$, the current level relative to the running maximum ($\le 0$ once the window has opened) |
| `wks_since_max` | $d_t = t - A_t$ |
| `g1` | $\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}$, one-week log growth |
| `g2` | $\ell_{t-1} - \ell_{t-2}$, the previous week's log growth |
| `g3` | $\ell_t - \ell_{t-3}$, three-week log growth |
| `rm3` | $\log\bigl(\operatorname{mean}\{\bar x_{t-2}, \bar x_{t-1}, \bar x_t\} + \varepsilon\bigr) - \ell^M_t$, the three-week mean level relative to the running maximum (mean over the available values) |
| `cum_rel` | $\log\bigl(\sum_{u=5}^{t} x_u + \varepsilon\bigr) - \ell^M_t$, cumulative incidence since season week 5 relative to the running maximum (missing $x_u$ count as 0) |
| `hist_rel` | $\ell^M_t - \bar P_{g,l,s}$, where $\bar P_{g,l,s}$ is the mean of $\log(Y^*_{s'} + \varepsilon)$ over the strictly earlier complete seasons $s' < s$ of the same source and location (missing if there are none) |
| `nat_rel_max`, `nat_wks_since_max`, `nat_g3` | `rel_max`, `wks_since_max` and `g3` of the national series of the same source and season (for a national series, its own values; missing if no national series exists) |
| `src_code` | source: 0 = NHSN, 1 = ILINet, 2 = FluSurv-NET |

GBQR uses all 13 features; KCDE uses a subset (@sec-kcde); the baseline uses only `season_week` and `wks_since_max`. For the current season, `hist_rel` uses the mean NHSN log peak over all training seasons of that location, which are exactly the strictly earlier ones, and the national features come from the US series of the same revision draw (@sec-backfill).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
The original plan reused the `idmodels` weekly-model feature machinery (Taylor-polynomial features on fourth-root, centered and scaled series; rolling means and lags; a Christmas indicator; one-hot aggregation level; $\log N_l$; the fraction of states past their maximum; the previous season's peak week). The implemented features are a smaller set of log ratios, chosen so that no scale factors are needed.
:::

## Avoiding leakage

**Leakage** means that information not available in real time enters the features or the fitting. The design addresses four possible sources.

1. **Transformation factors computed with future data.** Not applicable: no center-and-scale factors are used (@sec-transforms).
2. **Features computed on the full series.** Every feature at origin $t$ is computed from the series truncated at week $t$ (`state_features` only reads columns $1, \dots, t$), with strictly trailing windows.
3. **Final instead of real-time values.** Training deliberately uses final values for all sources, and the model is then applied to simulated final versions of the current season (@sec-backfill). The current season's real-time values are therefore never mistaken for final ones.
4. **The same epidemic in another source.** ILINet, FluSurv-NET and NHSN rows from the same calendar season describe the same epidemic. Forward chaining excludes the forecast season from every source. Inside training, the one procedure that validates on held-out data (KCDE bandwidth selection) holds out whole calendar seasons from all sources at once.

## Dependence between rows, and why we validate by season {#sec-loso}

The training rows are far from independent.

- **Within a (source, location, season).** Consecutive origins $t$ and $t+1$ have nearly the same features and the same season outcome: $W^*$ is identical, so $k_{t+1} = k_t - 1$ exactly, and $z_{t+1}$ is close to $z_t$.
- **Across locations in a season.** All locations in a season experience the same circulating viruses, so their peaks tend to occur within a few weeks of one another, and their sizes are correlated.
- **Across sources in a season.** As noted above, sources in the same calendar season observe the same epidemic.

The effective number of independent units for learning about season-level variation is therefore closer to the number of *calendar seasons* (a few dozen) than to the number of rows. This has three consequences.

**Validation must be by season.** Suppose we instead held out randomly chosen rows. For almost every held-out row, the training set would contain its neighbor from the same season one week earlier, with nearly identical features and the target shifted by exactly one week. Any model that memorizes neighbors would look excellent, and tuning parameters on such a score would drive the models toward overfitting. (For the kernel method of @sec-kcde, random-row validation would push the bandwidths toward zero for exactly this reason.)

Two season-based schemes are used. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set of calendar seasons, let $D_s$ be all rows (all sources and locations) from season $s$, and let $S(\widehat F, \text{outcome})$ be a loss (a negatively oriented score).

- **Forward chaining** (used for the backtest, @sec-eval). For each evaluation season $s$, fit the model to $\bigcup_{s' < s} D_{s'}$ and forecast season $s$ in real time. This mimics operational use exactly.
- **Leave-one-season-out (LOSO)** (used only inside training, to choose KCDE's bandwidths). For each row $i \in D_s$, the prediction $\widehat F_{-s}$ is formed with all rows of season $s$ removed. The LOSO estimate of predictive performance is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{CV}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|} \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} \frac{1}{|D_s|} \sum_{i \in D_s} S\bigl(\widehat{F}_{-s}(\cdot \mid \phi_i),\, \text{outcome}_i\bigr).
$$
LOSO treats seasons as exchangeable draws from a common population of seasons. That assumption is imperfect (reporting systems change, and the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted influenza), and because LOSO trains on seasons after the held-out one it can be somewhat optimistic, which is why the backtest uses forward chaining.

**Resampling should be by season.** Methods that resample data to reduce estimation variability (bagging in @sec-gbqr) resample whole seasons, not rows.

**Score comparisons should be blocked by season.** When comparing models on held-out forecasts, differences are strongly correlated within a season; standard errors should be computed treating seasons (not forecasts) as the independent units.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Excluded seasons and row weights.** The pandemic seasons 2008/09, 2009/10, 2020/21 and 2021/22 are excluded because `iddata` sets their values to missing (@sec-transforms). All training rows have equal weight in the baseline and GBQR; ILINet therefore contributes many more rows than NHSN. KCDE has one tuned parameter, $\lambda$, that down-weights analogs from a different source than the query row; for real forecasts the query is NHSN, so this down-weights ILINet and FluSurv-NET rows (@sec-kcde).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
Leave-one-season-out training for the backtest (with forward chaining only as a sensitivity check), and row weights giving each source a comparable total weight per season with NHSN up-weighted. Neither is implemented.
:::

# The models {#sec-models}

## A common output format, and from timing classes to a pmf {#sec-classes-to-pmf}

Every model is a map from a feature vector $\phi$ (computed at origin $t$) to

1. **timing:** probabilities $(\pi_0, \dots, \pi_{k_{\max}})$ for the timing classes $k^+ \in \{0, \dots, k_{\max}\}$, summing to 1; and
2. **size:** 23 nondecreasing values $\hat Q_z(\tau \mid \phi)$, $\tau \in \mathcal{T}$, estimating the quantiles of $z$.

These outputs pass through the same post-processing (`PeakModel._predict_current_season`): the backfill simulation and floor of @sec-backfill and the formatting of @sec-submission.

**Climatology.** Several steps use a **climatological** pmf $p_{\text{clim}}$, a smoothed version of the historical distribution of peak weeks. Let $i$ index the complete historical series (all sources and locations, training seasons only), with peak week $W^*_i$ and season $s(i)$, and let $n_s$ be the number of such series in season $s$. For $w \in \mathcal{W}$,
$$
p_{\text{clim}}(w) \propto \sum_i \frac{1}{n_{s(i)}}\; \frac{\exp\{-(w - W^*_i)^2 / (2 h_{\text{clim}}^2)\}}{\sum_{u \in \mathcal{W}} \exp\{-(u - W^*_i)^2 / (2 h_{\text{clim}}^2)\}},
$$
normalized to sum to 1 over the window. Each series contributes a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation $h_{\text{clim}}$ weeks, truncated and renormalized to the window. The weight $1/n_{s(i)}$ gives every season the same total weight, so that sources and seasons with many locations do not dominate. Smoothing avoids giving zero probability to weeks in which no historical peak happened to occur.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Climatology** (`series.peak_week_climatology`). $h_{\text{clim}} = 1.5$ weeks: `PeakModelConfig.timing_smoothing_sd = 1.5`, shared by all three models.
:::

**Allowed classes.** At origin $t$, class $j \ge 1$ is **allowed** if the week $t + j$ lies in the window, $\underline\omega \le t + j \le \overline\omega$. Class $0$ ("already peaked") is allowed only if $t \ge \underline\omega$, that is, once a window week has been reported. Disallowed classes are set to zero and the remaining probabilities are divided by their total. This renormalization simply conditions on an event we know to be certain (the peak lies in the window). Models trained on window-restricted targets already give these classes little probability, so the correction is small.

**Spreading by climatology.** For a model that does not distinguish classes beyond some $j_0 - 1$, the probability of "$k^+ \ge j_0$" is spread as
$$
\pi_j \;\propto\; p_{\text{clim}}(t + j), \qquad j \ge j_0,\; t + j \in \mathcal{W},
$$
normalized over those $j$ (`PeakModel._spread_climatology`). This is the conditional distribution of the peak week under climatology, given that the peak is at least $j_0$ weeks after $t$.

The class probabilities are mapped to window weeks in @sec-mc: class $j \ge 1$ to week $t + j$, and class $0$ to the week of the running maximum.

## Model 1: conditional climatology (`peak_baseline`) {#sec-baseline}

The baseline answers: "what would we predict using only the calendar and the crudest summary of the season so far?" Its metadata describe it as the FluSight baseline for these targets, and it is not designated (`designated_model: false`). Every other model must beat it to be worth using.

**Timing.** Let $b(d) = \min(d, 4)$ bin the weeks since the maximum into $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4{+}\}$. The baseline estimates the probability that the peak has already happened as a smoothed frequency among training rows with the same origin week and the same bin:
$$
\hat\pi_0(t, b) = \frac{\#\{i : t_i = t,\, b(d_i) = b,\, k_i \le 0\} + 0.5}{\#\{i : t_i = t,\, b(d_i) = b\} + 1},
$$
where $t_i$ and $d_i$ are the origin and weeks since the maximum of row $i$. The constants $0.5$ and $1$ make this the posterior mean under a Jeffreys Beta$(1/2, 1/2)$ prior, which keeps the estimate away from exactly 0 and 1. The forecast uses $\pi_0 = \hat\pi_0(t, b(d_t))$, with three exceptions: $\pi_0 = 0$ before the window opens ($t < \underline\omega$); $\pi_0 = 1$ if $t \ge \underline\omega$ and no future window week remains ($t \ge \overline\omega$); and $\pi_0 = 0.5$ if no training row has that $(t, b)$. The remaining probability is spread over the future window weeks by climatology:
$$
\pi_j = (1 - \pi_0)\, \frac{p_{\text{clim}}(t + j)}{\sum_{u \in \mathcal{W},\, u > t} p_{\text{clim}}(u)}, \qquad j \ge 1,\; t + j \in \mathcal{W}.
$$

**Size.** The quantiles of $z$ are the empirical quantiles of $z_i$ among training rows with $|t_i - t| \le 2$ and the same bin $b(d_i) = b(d_t)$. If fewer than 20 rows qualify, the bin is ignored and all rows with $|t_i - t| \le 2$ are used.

**Why.** It is cheap, transparent, and uses exactly the same conditioning as the other models. Improvements over it can be attributed to the information in the features rather than to the conditioning trick itself.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Baseline settings** (`baseline.py`, `PeakBaselineModelConfig`).

- $\hat\pi_0$ uses the exact season week $t$ (no neighborhood) and 5 bins of $d$ (`WSM_BINS = 5`, not configurable). For lookup, $t$ is clipped to the range of training origins, $[5, 43]$.
- Size neighborhood: `size_week_halfwidth = 2`; minimum stratum size 20 (hard-coded); quantiles by `numpy.quantile` (linear interpolation between order statistics).
- Climatology bandwidth: `timing_smoothing_sd = 1.5`.
- All sources are pooled with equal row weights.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
A season-week neighborhood for $\hat\pi_0$, strata defined by rising versus falling (the sign of a local slope) rather than by weeks since the maximum, and merging of small strata with neighboring weeks.
:::

## Model 2: gradient-boosted direct models (`peak_gbqr`) {#sec-gbqr}

This model (`PeakGBQRModel`) carries the approach of the lab's `GBQRModel` weekly model (`idmodels/gbqr.py`) over to the two peak targets.

### Quantile regression with the pinball loss

For a quantile level $\tau \in (0,1)$, the **pinball** (or check) loss is
$$
\ell_\tau(e) = e\,\bigl(\tau - \mathbf{1}\{e < 0\}\bigr) =
\begin{cases} \tau\, e & e \ge 0, \\ (\tau - 1)\, e & e < 0, \end{cases}
$$
applied to a residual $e = z - q$ (here $\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}$ is the indicator function). The key fact is that the minimizer over $q$ of the expected loss $\mathbb{E}[\ell_\tau(Z - q)]$ is a $\tau$-quantile of $Z$: for continuous $Z$ with distribution function $F_Z$, setting the derivative with respect to $q$ to zero gives $\tau - F_Z(q) = 0$. The same holds conditionally: over functions $f$, $\mathbb{E}[\ell_\tau(Z - f(\phi))]$ is minimized by the conditional quantile $f(\phi) = Q_Z(\tau \mid \phi)$ (Koenker and Bassett 1978). So fitting a flexible function by minimizing empirical pinball loss estimates a conditional quantile. The pinball loss handles the atom of $z$ at zero naturally: for $\tau$ below the conditional probability of the atom, the estimated quantile is (close to) zero.

**Gradient boosting** (Friedman 2001) fits $f$ as a sum of many small regression trees, adding one tree at a time to reduce the empirical loss. We use the LightGBM implementation (Ke et al. 2017) with `objective="quantile"`, fitting one model per quantile level $\tau \in \mathcal{T}$ to predict $z$ from all 13 features of @sec-features. LightGBM handles missing feature values natively (each tree split learns which side missing values go to), so rows with, for example, no earlier seasons (missing `hist_rel`) need no imputation.

**Where the boosting starts.** Boosting improves a starting prediction one small step at a time. By default LightGBM starts every row at the unconditional $\tau$-quantile of $z$ over all training rows. For upper levels that number is dominated by the very early-season rows discussed with @eq-z: the unconditional 97.5% quantile of $z$ is about 7.4. In post-peak states the correct 97.5% quantile is exactly 0, so the trees would have to pull the prediction down by more than 7 units, in steps shrunk by the learning rate. With the 100 trees and learning rate 0.05 used here they do not get there. The default model predicts about 0.98 for such states: a peak 2.7 times the observed maximum long after the season has turned, and so upper intervals far wider than necessary late in the season.

An option, `PeakGBQRModelConfig.size_offset = True` (sandbox model `peak_gbqr_offset`), starts each row from a sensible value instead. Each quantile regression is then boosted from an **offset** (LightGBM's `init_score`) equal to the conditional-climatology baseline's $\tau$-quantile of $z$ for that row (@sec-baseline), which already depends on the season week and on the weeks since the maximum. The trees learn only a correction to the baseline, and the prediction is the offset plus the boosted correction. On the training rows this brings the late-season 97.5% prediction to 0, while the early-season 97.5% quantile still covers about 99% of outcomes.

The offset is not the default, because it did not score better where it matters. In the 2023/24 to 2025/26 hindcasts:

- It improved the calibration of early-season intervals.
- It worsened the log-scale WIS of peak size overall (0.169 against 0.157), mostly for forecasts made one to four weeks after the peak.
- After the peak, where it tightens the intervals, the default's extra width mainly covered small late revisions to the reported peak and cost little.
- Adding trees (400 instead of 100) to fix the slow start instead was worse in held-out seasons, with or without the offset. With so few training seasons, more boosting overfits.

Both versions are kept so that combinations can be explored later. Peak-week forecasts are identical between them, because only the size regressions change.

### The timing classifier

A LightGBM classifier with a softmax output is trained on the grouped class
$$
\tilde k_i = \min(k^+_i, K + 1) \in \{0, 1, \dots, K, K+1\},
$$
where class $K + 1$ means "more than $K$ weeks ahead". It minimizes the multiclass cross-entropy $-\sum_i \log \hat\pi_{\tilde k_i}(\phi_i)$. This loss is the logarithmic score, which is strictly proper (@sec-eval), so minimizing it targets the true conditional class probabilities. At prediction, classes $0, \dots, K$ give $\pi_0, \dots, \pi_K$ directly, and the probability of class $K + 1$ is spread over the classes $j \ge K + 1$ by climatology (@sec-classes-to-pmf, with $j_0 = K + 1$).

### Bagging over seasons

The fit is repeated over $n_{\text{bag}}$ **bags**. For bag $\beta = 1, \dots, n_{\text{bag}}$, a random subset containing $\lfloor f_{\text{bag}} \cdot |\mathcal{S}_{\text{train}}| \rfloor$ of the training calendar seasons $\mathcal{S}_{\text{train}}$ is drawn without replacement, and all 23 quantile models and the timing classifier are fitted to the rows (all sources) from those seasons. **Bagging** (bootstrap aggregation, Breiman 1996) reduces the variance of an unstable learner such as boosted trees. Resampling whole seasons rather than rows matches the dependence structure of @sec-loso and prevents any single unusual season from dominating. Bagging stabilizes the *estimated* quantile function and class probabilities; the predictive spread itself comes from the quantile regressions and the classifier.

**Combining quantiles.** The quantile at level $\tau$ is the median, across bags, of the bag-specific predictions. Separately fitted quantile models can **cross** (a lower level having a larger predicted value), so the 23 medians are then sorted within each forecast, as in `_quantile_noncrossing` (`gbqr.py`). Sorting (monotone rearrangement) can only help. Writing $\ell_\tau(y - q) = \tau(y - q) + (q - y)^+$, where $(v)^+ = \max(v, 0)$, one can check that for levels $\tau_1 < \tau_2$ with crossed values $q_1 > q_2$, swapping the two values lowers $\ell_{\tau_1}(y - q_1) + \ell_{\tau_2}(y - q_2)$ by exactly $(\tau_2 - \tau_1)(q_1 - q_2) > 0$, whatever the outcome $y$. So sorting reduces the total pinball loss (and hence the weighted interval score of @sec-eval) for every outcome; see also Chernozhukov, Fernández-Val and Galichon (2010). Because @eq-z-invert is increasing, sorting in $z$ gives sorted quantiles of $Y^*$.

**Combining class probabilities.** Class probabilities are **averaged** across bags (a class absent from a bag's training rows receives probability 0 from that bag). Averaging, unlike a median, gives probabilities that still sum to one. Because the logarithm is concave, Jensen's inequality gives $\log\bigl(\frac{1}{n_{\text{bag}}}\sum_\beta \pi^{(\beta)}_j\bigr) \ge \frac{1}{n_{\text{bag}}}\sum_\beta \log \pi^{(\beta)}_j$ (with $\pi^{(\beta)}_j$ the probability of class $j$ from bag $\beta$), so the log score of the averaged forecast is never worse than the average log score of the bags. Averaging also tends to temper overconfident individual fits.

**Strengths and weaknesses.** GBQR uses the full feature set and the cross-source history directly, and bagging by season stabilizes it. Timing and size are modeled separately, so the two outputs do not come from one joint distribution; FluSight scores them separately, so this is acceptable. Tree models can be miscalibrated, so the backtest includes calibration checks (@sec-eval).

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**GBQR settings** (`gbqr.py`, `PeakGBQRModelConfig`).

- $n_{\text{bag}}$ = `num_bags` = 25 (3 with `--short_run`); $f_{\text{bag}}$ = `bag_frac_samples` = 0.7 (at least one season per bag).
- $K$ = `max_k` = 12, so the classifier has $K + 2 = 14$ classes.
- LightGBM: `n_estimators = 100`, `learning_rate = 0.05`, `min_child_samples = 50`; all other hyperparameters at LightGBM defaults; `src_code` treated as categorical.
- Per bag, 23 `LGBMRegressor(objective="quantile", alpha=τ)` models and one `LGBMClassifier(objective="multiclass")`.
- Aggregation: median across bags then sort (quantiles); mean across bags (class probabilities).
- Seeds: the random number generator is seeded with a CRC-32 hash of the sorted list of training seasons, so the fit is deterministic for a given set of training seasons (it does not depend on the reference date).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
**A hazard (continuation-ratio) timing model.** The ordered structure of $k$ can instead be modeled sequentially. Let $\pi_0(\phi) = \Pr(k \le 0 \mid \phi)$, and for $m \ge 1$ let the **discrete hazard** be $\chi_m(\phi) = \Pr(k = m \mid k \ge m,\, \phi)$, the probability that the peak is $m$ weeks ahead given that it is not earlier. Then
$$
\Pr(k = m \mid \phi) = \bigl(1 - \pi_0(\phi)\bigr)\, \chi_m(\phi) \prod_{m' = 1}^{m - 1}\bigl(1 - \chi_{m'}(\phi)\bigr).
$$
This is a continuation-ratio model for an ordinal response, equivalent to a discrete-time survival model (Tutz and Schmid 2016). It could be fitted with one binary classifier for $\pi_0$ and one for $\chi$, expanding each row with $k_i \ge 1$ into binary rows for $m = 1, \dots, \min(k_i, K + 1)$. Because the hazard is shared across offsets it pools information across nearby $m$. Not implemented. Also considered: $n_{\text{bag}} = 100$ and LightGBM default hyperparameters (the `GBQRModelConfig` weekly-model settings), and seeds derived from the reference date.
:::

## Model 3: kernel conditional density estimation (`peak_kcde`) {#sec-kcde}

This model is a nonparametric **analog** forecaster: it finds historical situations that look like the current one and uses what happened next in those situations as the forecast. It follows the kernel conditional density estimation (KCDE) approach of Ray, Sakrejda, Lauer, Johansson and Reich (2017), who used it to forecast seasonal targets including peak timing and peak incidence. They applied KCDE to weekly incidence at each horizon and combined horizons into trajectories with a copula. Here we apply the same kernel-weighting idea directly to the peak targets $(k^+, z)$.

### State vector

The state of a season at origin $t$ is the 7-vector $\phi$ of the features `season_week`, `rel_max`, $\min(d_t, 10)$ (`wks_since_max` capped at 10), `g1`, `g3`, `rm3` and `nat_rel_max`, where a missing `nat_rel_max` is replaced by the row's own `rel_max`. Training rows with any other of these features missing are dropped. Each component is standardized with the training mean and standard deviation, $\tilde\phi_\iota = (\phi_\iota - \bar\phi_\iota)/\mathrm{sd}_\iota$ for components $\iota = 1, \dots, 7$; a query component that is still missing is set to 0 (the training mean).

### Kernel weights

Every training row $i$ with $|t_i - t'| \le 4$, where $t' = \min\{\max(t, \min_i t_i), \max_i t_i\}$ is $t$ clipped to the range of training origins, is a candidate analog. It receives the weight
$$
\kappa_i(\phi) = \lambda^{\mathbf{1}\{g_i \ne g\}} \prod_{\iota=1}^{7} \exp\left\{-\frac12\left(\frac{\tilde\phi_\iota - \tilde\phi_{i,\iota}}{h_\iota}\right)^2\right\},
\qquad
\varpi_i(\phi) = \frac{\kappa_i(\phi)}{\sum_{i'} \kappa_{i'}(\phi)},
$$
where $g_i$ is the source of row $i$ and $g$ is the source of the query (NHSN for every real forecast; the source of the tuning row during bandwidth selection), $h_\iota > 0$ is the **bandwidth** for component $\iota$ (on the standardized scale; unrelated to the forecast horizon $h$ of @sec-problem), and $\lambda \in (0, 1]$ is a **source discount** for analogs from a different source than the query. Defining the discount relative to the query's source, rather than relative to NHSN, makes bandwidth selection consistent with prediction: when a tuning row is an ILINet row, its same-source analogs play the role that NHSN analogs play for an NHSN query. The sum in $\varpi_i$ runs over the candidate analogs. This is a Gaussian product kernel: each component has its own bandwidth, so the data can decide that, for example, the level relative to the maximum must match closely while growth may differ more. The hard restriction to origins within 4 weeks, on top of the kernel in `season_week`, keeps the analogs at a similar stage of the season and limits computation. The source factor is the kernel of Aitchison and Aitken (1976) for a categorical variable, it equals 1 for the same source and $\lambda$ for a different one.

### Weighted analog predictive distributions

The weighted analog outcomes define a joint predictive distribution of $(k^+, z)$ (a Nadaraya–Watson-type estimator of a conditional distribution; Hyndman, Bashtannyk and Grunwald 1996), whose two marginals are used:

- **timing:** $\pi^{\text{A}}_j(\phi) = \sum_i \varpi_i(\phi)\, \mathbf{1}\{k^+_i = j\}$, $j = 0, \dots, k_{\max}$. KCDE uses the exact offsets, without grouping into a tail class.
- **size:** the weighted empirical distribution function $F^{\text{A}}(v \mid \phi) = \sum_i \varpi_i(\phi) \mathbf{1}\{z_i \le v\}$, whose atom at zero comes from analogs that had already peaked.

### Mixing with the baseline

Analog methods fail badly when the current season looks unlike anything in the history, because the weights then concentrate on a few poor analogs. To guard against this, the forecast is a mixture with the baseline of @sec-baseline, fitted to the same training rows, with weight $\eta$:
$$
\pi_j = (1 - \eta)\, \pi^{\text{A}}_j + \eta\, \pi^{\text{base}}_j, \qquad F = (1 - \eta) F^{\text{A}} + \eta F^{\text{base}}.
$$
For size, the mixture is computed on discretized versions of the two distributions. The analog distribution is represented by its weighted quantiles $q^{\text{A}}(\tau') = \inf\{v : F^{\text{A}}(v \mid \phi) \ge \tau'\}$ on the 99-level grid $\tau' \in \{0.01, 0.02, \dots, 0.99\}$, each given mass $(1-\eta)/99$; the baseline by its 23 quantiles $q^{\text{base}}(\tau)$, each given mass $\eta/23$. The output quantile at level $\tau \in \mathcal{T}$ is the $\tau$-quantile $\inf\{v : \hat F(v) \ge \tau\}$ of this 122-point discrete distribution $\hat F$.

### Bandwidth selection by leave-one-season-out log score

The parameters $\theta = (\log h_1, \dots, \log h_7, \log\lambda)$ are chosen to maximize the leave-one-season-out log score of the **timing class** on a tuning set $\mathcal{Q}$ of training rows:
$$
\hat\theta = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta}\; \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{Q}} \log\Bigl[(1 - \eta)\, \bar\pi^{\text{A}, -s(i)}_{k^+_i}(\phi_i; \theta) + \eta\, \bar\pi^{\text{base}}_{k^+_i}(\phi_i) + 10^{-12}\Bigr].
$$
Here $\bar\pi^{\text{A}, -s(i)}$ is the analog timing distribution for row $i$ computed with every row of $i$'s calendar season $s(i)$ (all sources and locations) removed from its analogs; both components are restricted to the allowed classes at $t_i$ and renormalized (if all analog weights vanish, the analog part is uniform over the allowed classes). The source discount is capped at 1 by using $\lambda = \exp\{\min(\theta_8, 0)\}$. As explained in @sec-loso, leaving out whole seasons is essential: otherwise the best analog for every row is its own season one week earlier, and the chosen bandwidths collapse toward zero. The size part does not enter the objective; it uses the bandwidths chosen for timing.

**Strengths and weaknesses.** KCDE has few parameters, its timing and size come from the same analogs, and it works well when the current season resembles past ones. It is methodologically very different from GBQR, which is why the two are both designated. Its main weakness is seasons without good analogs; the mixture weight $\eta$ addresses the worst consequences.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**KCDE settings** (`kcde.py`, `PeakKCDEModelConfig`).

- Analog window: `sw_radius = 4` season weeks.
- Mixture weight: $\eta$ = `baseline_mix` = 0.05, for both timing and size.
- Tuning set: `num_tuning_rows` = 2000 rows drawn without replacement with a fixed seed, up to half of them NHSN rows and the rest ILINet and FluSurv-NET rows.
- Optimizer: Nelder–Mead (`scipy.optimize.minimize`) from $h_\iota = 0.5$ for all $\iota$ and $\lambda = 0.5$, with an initial simplex of unit steps on the log scale ($\theta_0$ and $\theta_0 + e_\iota$ for each coordinate direction $e_\iota$), at most `max_tuning_iter` = 200 iterations (10 with `--short_run`), `xatol = 1e-2`, `fatol = 1e-4`.
- The fitted bandwidths on the original feature scales, $h_\iota\,\mathrm{sd}_\iota$, are stored as `bandwidths_`, and the tuning log score as `tuning_score_`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternatives considered"}
A state vector containing the recent trajectory shape $\bigl(\log\{(x_{t-n} + \varepsilon)/(M_t + \varepsilon)\}\bigr)_{n = 0, \dots, 3}$ and $\log(1 + d_t)$; kernel smoothing of the size distribution in $z$ with an outcome bandwidth; a joint timing-and-size LOSO objective; L-BFGS optimization from a rule-of-thumb start; joint $(k, z)$ draws for the backfill simulation; and a warning when the **effective number of analogs**, $n_{\text{eff}} = 1 / \sum_i \varpi_i^2$, is small. None of these is implemented, although $n_{\text{eff}}$ remains a useful diagnostic.
:::

## Model 4 (planned): Bayesian hierarchical model of timing and size (`peak_hier`) {#sec-hier}

::: {.callout-warning title="Planned, not implemented"}
This model is a design only. No code exists yet, and none of its settings below have been tested.
:::

This optional model makes the strongest structural assumption: that locations in the same season share a common season-level tendency in timing and size, and that the same location tends to behave similarly across seasons. It would be implemented in NumPyro (Phan, Pradhan and Jankowiak 2019), which the lab already uses for SARIX models.

### Likelihood

Index training rows by $i = (g, l, s, t)$. **Timing** would use the continuation-ratio (hazard) form described under *Alternatives considered* in @sec-gbqr:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit} \pi_{0, i} &= \beta_0^\top \phi_i + u^{0}_l + v^{0}_s, \\
\operatorname{logit} \chi_{i,m} &= f_\omega(t_i+m) + f_m(m) + \beta^\top \phi_i + u_l + v_s + \gamma_g ,
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\{p/(1-p)\}$, $\chi_{i,m}$ is the discrete hazard of row $i$ at offset $m$, the feature vector $\phi_i$ includes a constant (intercept) term, $\beta_0$ and $\beta$ are coefficient vectors, $f_\omega$ is a smooth function of the season week $t_i + m$ of the candidate peak week, $f_m$ is a smooth function of the offset $m$, $\gamma_g$ is a source effect, $u_l$ is a **location effect**, and $v_s$ is a **season effect** shared by all locations in season $s$; $u^0_l$ and $v^0_s$ are the corresponding effects for the already-peaked probability, with their own normal distributions and variances.

**Size** would be modeled only for rows whose peak is still to come ($k_i \ge 1$), since for $k_i \le 0$ the size is determined by the atom at $z = 0$:
$$
z_i \mid k_i \ge 1 \;\sim\; \operatorname{St}_{\nu}\bigl(\mu_i,\, \sigma_g(t_i)\bigr) \text{ truncated to } (0, \infty),
\qquad
\mu_i = \beta_z^\top \phi_i + u^z_l + v^z_s ,
$$
where $\operatorname{St}_{\nu}(\mu, \sigma)$ is a Student-$t$ distribution with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$; $\beta_z$ is a coefficient vector; $u^z_l$ and $v^z_s$ are location and season effects for size; and the scale $\sigma_g(t)$ depends on the source and varies smoothly with the origin week. The heavy tails of the $t$ distribution let occasional very large seasons occur without distorting the fit for typical seasons. The location and season effects of the two parts are allowed to be correlated:
$$
(u_l, u^z_l)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_{\text{loc}}), \qquad (v_s, v^z_s)^\top \sim \mathcal{N}_2(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_{\text{sea}}),
$$
where $\mathcal{N}_2(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma)$ is a bivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix $\Sigma$. So, for example, seasons that peak early could also tend to be large, if the data support it.

### Partial pooling

The random effects implement **partial pooling**. Consider the simplest case: $n_l$ independent observations for location $l$ with mean $\bar z_l$, observation variance $\sigma^2$, and a location effect $u^z_l \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_a^2)$ around a common mean $\mu$, with $\mu$, $\sigma^2$ and $\sigma_a^2$ treated as known. The posterior mean of the effect is
$$
\mathbb{E}[u^z_l \mid \text{data}] = B_l\, (\bar z_l - \mu), \qquad B_l = \frac{n_l / \sigma^2}{n_l/\sigma^2 + 1/\sigma_a^2} \in (0, 1).
$$
With much data about location $l$ ($n_l$ large), $B_l \to 1$ and the estimate follows that location's own data (no pooling). With little data, $B_l \to 0$ and the estimate is shrunk toward the common mean (complete pooling). The variance $\sigma_a^2$ is estimated from the data, so how much to shrink is itself learned. This matters here because the NHSN history per location is only a few seasons long.

Two cautions apply. First, replay rows from the same season are not independent observations, so $n_l$ in this formula should be thought of as roughly the number of seasons, not the number of rows. The season effects $v_s$ and $v^z_s$ help here: they absorb deviations shared by all rows of a season, so that the 39 replay rows of one season are not treated as 39 independent pieces of evidence. A (location, season) effect can be added for the same reason. Second, source-specific scales $\sigma_g$ and source effects $\gamma_g$ keep the many ILINet rows from overwhelming the few NHSN rows.

### Using the current season: censored observations

The season effect $v_s$ captures the strongest signal available to a peak forecaster: states in the same season peak at similar times, so states that have already peaked carry information about states that have not. But in a model that conditions on features, a *new* season's effect $v_{s_0}$ is learned only if some likelihood term involves the current season. Such terms can be obtained from **censoring**, as in survival analysis. Ignoring revisions, at time $t$ in the current season $s_0$ we know for each location $l$ that $W^*_l \ge A_{l,t}$ (the subscript $l$ is restored here because several locations are involved), since no past non-maximal week can be the peak. For each earlier origin $t' < A_{l,t}$ in the current season this means $k_{t'} \ge A_{l,t} - t'$: a right-censored observation of the timing offset, contributing
$$
\Pr(k_{t'} \ge A_{l,t} - t' \mid \phi_{t'}) = \bigl(1 - \pi_{0}(\phi_{t'})\bigr) \prod_{m=1}^{A_{l,t} - t' - 1} \bigl(1 - \chi_m(\phi_{t'})\bigr)
$$
to the likelihood. Similarly $Y^*_l \ge M_{l,t}$ gives a lower bound on $z_{t'}$. These terms involve $v_{s_0}$ and $v^z_{s_0}$, so the posterior of the current season's effects is updated by what every location has shown so far, without using any unavailable information.

### Priors and inference

Features would be standardized, and the priors weakly informative: normal priors with unit scale on regression coefficients, half-normal priors on standard deviations of random effects (Gelman 2006), an LKJ prior on the correlation matrices in $\Sigma_{\text{loc}}$ and $\Sigma_{\text{sea}}$ (Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe 2009), second-order random-walk priors on $f_\omega$ and $f_m$, and a Gamma(2, 0.1) prior on $\nu$. The posterior would be sampled with the No-U-Turn Sampler (Hoffman and Gelman 2014), with the standard convergence diagnostics ($\hat R$, effective sample size, divergent transitions). Posterior predictive draws of $(k, z)$ are obtained by drawing parameters from the posterior, then $k$ from its class probabilities, then $z$ given $k$.

**Why it matters, and its cost.** It would be the only model in which the within-season shared effect is explicit and in which uncertainty about all parameters propagates into full joint draws. The tree and analog models capture season synchrony only indirectly, through the national features. It is also the most work to build and to tune, and it will be built only if the backtest shows that models 2 and 3 are missing this structure.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Not implemented.** Proposed specification: the hurdle structure above (size likelihood only for $k \ge 1$, truncated at zero), the censored current-season terms, and the priors listed above; NUTS with 4 chains, with warm-up and sample sizes to be set after pilot runs. Because training rows use final data, $k_i \ge 1$ implies $z_i > 0$ whenever $t_i \ge \underline\omega$; rows before the window opens can have $k_i \ge 1$ and $z_i \le 0$, and would need a size likelihood that is not truncated at zero.
:::

## Model 5 (planned): ensembles (`peak_ensemble`) {#sec-ensemble}

::: {.callout-warning title="Planned, not implemented"}
No ensemble of the peak models has been built yet. This section records the planned combination rules.
:::

Combining forecasts from different models usually improves accuracy and robustness. The two targets would be combined differently, because they are different types of forecast.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the set of component models, indexed by $\mathfrak{m}$, with weights $\vartheta_{\mathfrak m} \ge 0$ and $\sum_{\mathfrak m \in \mathcal{M}} \vartheta_{\mathfrak m} = 1$.

**Peak week: linear pool.** For component pmfs $p^{\mathfrak m}$,
$$
p^{\text{ens}}(w) = \sum_{\mathfrak m \in \mathcal{M}} \vartheta_{\mathfrak m} \, p^{\mathfrak m}(w).
$$
The result is again a pmf, and if every component puts at least some value $\delta' > 0$ on every week, then so does the pool. A linear pool of calibrated but different forecasts tends to be somewhat too wide (Ranjan and Gneiting 2010); if the components are overconfident, as flexible models fitted to few seasons can be, this is not necessarily a disadvantage.

**Peak size: quantile averaging.** For component quantiles $q^{\mathfrak m}(\tau)$,
$$
q^{\text{ens}}(\tau) = \sum_{\mathfrak m \in \mathcal{M}} \vartheta_{\mathfrak m} \, q^{\mathfrak m}(\tau).
$$
This is also called **Vincentization**. An average of nondecreasing functions of $\tau$ is nondecreasing, so the result is a valid set of quantiles. Compared with pooling the distributions, quantile averaging keeps the typical spread of the components rather than widening it (Lichtendahl, Grushka-Cockayne and Winkler 2013). This matches the behavior of `hubEnsembles::simple_ensemble()`, used by the `flu_flusion` model, whose default aggregation is the mean: for pmf outputs it averages probabilities (a linear pool) and for quantile outputs it averages quantiles.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Not implemented.** Planned: equal weights over the component models that beat the baseline in the backtest, with weights learned from the backtest only if the backtest supports it; the floor of @sec-floor re-applied after pooling; quantile averages rounded to integers after averaging (@sec-submission).
:::

# Backfill and the probabilities of past weeks {#sec-backfill}

## Why past weeks need positive probability

Suppose that at time $t$ the currently reported maximum is at week $A_t$, and another past week $w \ne A_t$ is currently reported slightly lower. Under final data it could not be the peak, but with revisions it might: if week $w$ is later revised upward (or week $A_t$ downward) enough that its final value exceeds that of every other window week, it becomes the peak. If a model gives such a week probability exactly zero and it does become the peak, the log score (@sec-eval) of that forecast is $\log 0 = -\infty$, and so is any average that includes it. A single such event would make a model's average log score infinitely bad. More importantly, putting zero on a possible outcome is simply a wrong statement of uncertainty.

All models therefore share one post-processing step (`PeakModel._predict_current_season`), which (1) estimates how NHSN counts are revised, (2) simulates plausible final versions of the current season and applies the model to each, and (3) applies a floor to every window week.

## The revision model: a block bootstrap of revision vectors {#sec-revision}

Revisions are measured on **counts**. For location $l$, a vintage $a$ and a lag $j$, let $w = t_l(a) - j$ and define the **log revision ratio**
$$
\rho_{l,a,j} = \log \frac{c^{(a^\dagger)}_{l,w} + 1}{c^{(a)}_{l,w} + 1},
$$
where $a^\dagger$ is the latest vintage with as-of date on or before the reference date $r$, which serves as "final". It is positive if the week was revised upward after lag $j$, and zero if it was not revised. The offset $1$ keeps the ratio finite for zero counts. For each (vintage, location) pair we record the **revision vector** $\boldsymbol\rho_{l,a} = (\rho_{l,a,0}, \dots, \rho_{l,a,J-1})$ over the $J$ most recent weeks of that release.

Revisions of different weeks in one release are dependent: for example, a batch of late hospital reports raises the whole recent tail of a series together. Instead of modeling this dependence, the implementation resamples **whole vectors**, a form of block bootstrap: a draw of the revisions of the current release is a randomly chosen historical revision vector, which automatically carries the lag profile and the within-release dependence. Small counts are revised proportionally more, so vectors are grouped into **strata** by the reported lag-0 count $c^{(a)}_{l, t_l(a)}$, and the current release of location $l$ draws from the stratum of its own lag-0 count.

::: {.callout-note title="Implementation"}
**Revision model** (`revision.RevisionModel`, `revision.load_nhsn_vintages`).

- **Vintages.** All NHSN vintages (HHS archive before 2024-11-15, NHSN afterwards) with as-of date $\le r$, loaded as counts (`NHSNDataSource(rates=False)`); a few snapshots with a different file schema are skipped.
- **Lags.** $J$ = `PeakModelConfig.revision_max_lag` = 10, lags $j = 0, \dots, 9$ relative to each vintage's latest week for that location. Weeks at lag 10 or more are treated as final.
- **Maturity.** Only vintages with as-of date at least $J$ weeks before $a^\dagger$ are used, so that every recorded week has had at least 10 weeks to mature. Vectors with any lag missing are dropped. Vectors from all times of year and all locations (including the US) are pooled.
- **Strata.** Lag-0 count $< 50$, $[50, 500)$, and $\ge 500$ (`strata_bounds = (50, 500)`). If a location's stratum has fewer than 30 vectors (`min_stratum_vectors`), all vectors are used.
